topic: JVM Internals (Memory Model, G1/ZGC, Class Loading)

questions.question: What is the primary cause of the `Metaspace` memory leak in this code?
options: A) The `activeLoaders` map retains strong references to `URLClassLoader`, which prevents the JVM GC from reclaiming class metadata.
B) The `GlobalRegistry` retains a strong reference to `pluginInstance`, which keeps its `Class` object and consequently its `URLClassLoader` reachable and uncollectable.
C) Metaspace cannot garbage-collect dynamically instantiated `URLClassLoader` objects unless `System.gc()` is explicitly invoked inside `unload`.
D) Metaspace allocations are non-reclaimable by design in standard HotSpot JVM executions when running with `-XX:+UseG1GC`.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) The `GlobalRegistry` retains a strong reference to `pluginInstance`, which keeps its `Class` object and consequently its `URLClassLoader` reachable and uncollectable.
questions.explanation: In Java's ClassLoader architecture, a custom `ClassLoader` can only be garbage collected if ALL classes loaded by it and ALL instances of those classes are unreachable. Because `GlobalRegistry` retains a strong reference to `pluginInstance`, `pluginInstance.getClass()` remains reachable, which maintains a strong reference back to `childLoader`. As a result, none of the plugin's metadata in `Metaspace` can be reclaimed.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a low-latency trading microservice running on JDK 17 with `ZGC` (`-XX:+UseZGC`) experiences sudden latency spikes exceeding 150ms during high-volume spikes. GC logs reveal messages indicating `Allocation Stall` events occurring on multiple application threads.
questions.question: What is the underlying JVM mechanic triggering these allocation stalls, and how should it be remediated?
options: A) Application threads are allocating memory faster than `ZGC` can concurrently mark and relocate memory, forcing application threads to pause; solved by increasing heap size (`-Xmx`) or tuning `-XX:ConcGCThreads`.
B) `ZGC` hit a severe memory fragmentation limit and fell back to a single-threaded Stop-The-World (STW) compaction phase; solved by switching to `G1GC`.
C) Thread-Local Allocation Buffers (TLABs) became exhausted, forcing memory allocations to contend on heavy OS locks; solved by setting `-XX:-UseTLAB`.
D) Read barriers executed colored pointer checks that suffered cache misses across NUMA sockets; solved by setting `-XX:-UseNUMA`.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Application threads are allocating memory faster than `ZGC` can concurrently mark and relocate memory, forcing application threads to pause; solved by increasing heap size (`-Xmx`) or tuning `-XX:ConcGCThreads`.
questions.explanation: `ZGC` performs almost all GC tasks concurrently with application threads. However, if the allocation rate of application threads outpaces the rate at which concurrent GC worker threads can free memory, the heap becomes full. When this occurs, threads trying to allocate memory suffer an `Allocation Stall` (a pause) until GC progress frees up available space. Remediation includes increasing heap size (`-Xmx`), allocating more concurrent GC threads (`-XX:ConcGCThreads`), or tuning allocation rates.

questions.question: What is the primary cause of the transaction failing to roll back?
options: A) Spring's `@Transactional` annotation does not trigger rollbacks for `RuntimeException` unless `rollbackFor = Throwable.class` is defined.
B) Self-invocation (`this.saveOrderWithTransaction(...)`) calls the method directly on the internal target instance, bypassing the Spring AOP Proxy and transaction interceptor.
C) The JVM JIT compiler inlined `saveOrderWithTransaction` into `processOrder`, stripping out the bytecode instructions for transactional boundaries.
D) `@Service` beans use JDK Dynamic Proxies by default, which can only intercept methods declared on interfaces.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Self-invocation (`this.saveOrderWithTransaction(...)`) calls the method directly on the internal target instance, bypassing the Spring AOP Proxy and transaction interceptor.
questions.explanation: Spring's declarative transaction management relies on AOP dynamic proxies (CGLIB or JDK Dynamic Proxies). When a method inside the target class invokes another method (`saveOrderWithTransaction`) directly on `this`, the call bypasses the Spring Proxy wrapper completely. Consequently, the `@Transactional` advice interceptor is never invoked, no database transaction is created, and no rollback occurs.
